title: Tarn Hollow
raw_wikitext:
'''Tarn Hollow''' is a small glacial lake in the Wetherby uplands. It lies at the head of a steep valley and is fed by two streams that rise on the surrounding moorland. The lake is roughly oval in shape and is enclosed on three sides by cliffs of dark volcanic rock. Walkers usually reach it by a stone path that climbs from the hamlet of Low Garth, a journey of about two hours.

The water is cold and clear throughout the year, and it supports a small population of brown trout. Naturalists have recorded several species of dragonfly along the northern shore, where a belt of sedge provides shelter from the wind. In winter the surface often freezes for several weeks, and the valley below can be cut off by snow.

title: Aldermoor Lighthouse
raw_wikitext:
'''Aldermoor Lighthouse''' is a lighthouse located in the northern coast of Verran. It is regarded as one of the most notable examples of maritime navigation in the region, and it has been studied by local historians for several generations. The site is best known for its granite tower and its rotating lens, both of which survive in largely original condition and attract a steady number of visitors every year.

== History ==
Construction began after a public subscription raised the necessary funds, and the first phase of work was finished within six years. Early records describe the fog signal in considerable detail, noting that skilled workers were brought from neighbouring districts to complete it. During the following decades the lighthouse was enlarged twice, and the keeper's cottage were added as part of the second enlargement. A period of decline followed when funding was withdrawn, but a preservation society later took over its care.

== Present day ==
Today Aldermoor Lighthouse is managed by a charitable trust that organises guided tours and publishes an annual report on maritime navigation. Volunteers maintain the granite tower throughout the year, while specialists inspect the rotating lens every spring. The trust has also digitised its archive, so researchers can consult drawings of the fog signal and photographs of the keeper's cottage without travelling to the northern coast of Verran.

title: Tarn Hollow
raw_wikitext:
'''Tarn Hollow''' is a small glacial lake in the Wetherby uplands. It lies at the head of a steep valley and is fed by two streams that rise on the surrounding moorland. The lake is roughly oval in shape and is enclosed on three sides by cliffs of dark volcanic rock. Walkers usually reach it by a stone path that climbs from the hamlet of Low Garth, a journey of about two hours.

The water is cold and clear throughout the year, and it supports a small population of brown trout. Naturalists have recorded several species of dragonfly along the northern shore, where a belt of sedge provides shelter from the wind. In winter the surface often freezes for several weeks, and the valley below can be cut off by snow.

== Geology ==
The basin was carved by ice during the last glacial period, and a ridge of moraine still dams the outflow. Geologists from the regional survey mapped the cliffs in detail and identified three separate lava flows, each separated by a thin layer of ash. Samples taken from the lake bed contain pollen that records how the surrounding vegetation changed after the ice retreated. Birch and juniper appeared first, followed by oak woodland, and finally by the open heath that covers the slopes today. The survey also measured the depth of the lake, which reaches nineteen metres near the western cliff.

[[File:Quillon harbour view.jpg|thumb|The inner basin at low tide]]
'''Quillon Harbour''' is a fishing town on the western shore of [[Verran]]. It grew around a natural inlet that offered shelter to small boats, and by the end of the eighteenth century it had become the main [[herring]] port of the district.<ref>Local Gazetteer, 1802, p. 44.</ref> The town is built on two terraces above the quay, and most of its older houses are faced with pale limestone.

== Economy ==
Fishing remains the largest employer, although tourism has grown steadily since the coastal road was improved.<ref name="report">{{cite report |title=District Economic Survey |year=1998}}</ref> A boatyard on the northern side of the inlet repairs wooden vessels and trains apprentices in traditional methods. Several small smokehouses still cure fish over oak chips and sell their produce at the weekly market.

title: Tarn Hollow
raw_wikitext:
'''Tarn Hollow''' is a protected glacial lake in the Wetherby uplands, designated as a nature reserve. It lies at the head of a steep valley and is fed by two streams that rise on the surrounding moorland. Access is limited to a single marked path from the hamlet of Low Garth, and camping on the shore is not permitted. The reserve is managed by a county wildlife trust, which monitors the brown trout population and the dragonflies that breed along the northern shore.

Wardens visit the lake every week between April and October. They record water temperature, repair the path after heavy rain, and advise walkers about nesting birds on the cliffs. A short annual report summarises these observations for the public.
